narrative:
The 2025 Chicago White Sox entered the season carrying the wounds of a historically bad 2024 campaign, and Opening Day provided little reason for optimism. From the very first meaningful moment — Brooks Baldwin grounding into a double play to kill a rally — the Sox were a team that seemed to find new ways to lose. Their bullpen, anchored by the likes of Jordan Leasure and Steven Wilson, became a recurring source of heartbreak, surrendering leads and momentum at the worst possible moments through April and May. Luis Urías homering off Leasure in late April summarized the early months perfectly: a team too thin in pitching, too inconsistent at the plate, and too unlucky to string wins together.

June offered a fleeting glimpse of something better. Michael A. Taylor's clutch double on June 14th and Andrew Benintendi's grand slam on June 19th — his seventh of the year — gave South Side fans brief cause for excitement. Miguel Vargas and Kyle Teel also contributed timely hits in late June, and for a stretch it felt like the offense might be finding its footing. But the team's underlying numbers told the real story: a .675 OPS and a rotation that could not consistently keep opponents off the board meant that even the brightest moments were islands in a sea of losses.

July and August saw the White Sox gradually sink toward mathematical elimination. Freddie Freeman and Shohei Ohtani torched Steven Wilson in early July, while Aaron Civale surrendered crushing home runs to Kyle Manzardo and Royce Lewis in back-to-back starts in late July and August. Colson Montgomery's pop-up double play in foul territory on August 22nd — wiping out a potential rally in the same game Lewis hit a grand slam — crystallized the season's cruel rhythms. Even when individual players flashed potential, the team as a whole could not hold together long enough to matter.

September brought the curtain call on another lost season, punctuated by two wildly different moments on the same late date. Brandon Eisert walked in a run with a wild pitch against the Yankees, and Steven Wilson surrendered a go-ahead single to Aaron Judge's crew, hammering the coffin shut on any slim remaining hope. Yet Colson Montgomery — the 20-year-old shortstop who represents the organization's most tangible future asset — closed the book on 2025 with a two-run homer on September 26th, his 20th of the year, an exclamation point on a season otherwise defined by suffering. A 60-102 record told the story in full, but Montgomery's swing whispered that something worth watching might be coming.

chapters.title: Same Old Story
chapters.description: The Sox stumble out of the gate, with the bullpen and offense failing in tandem through the first two months.

chapters.title: A Glimmer in June
chapters.description: Taylor, Benintendi, Vargas, and Teel string together clutch hits, offering a rare stretch of hope on the South Side.

chapters.title: Sinking in Summer
chapters.description: July and August grind the White Sox down as the pitching staff surrenders game after critical game to contenders.

chapters.title: One Bright Spot
chapters.description: Michael A. Taylor delivers a season-high WPA double in early September before the losses pile back up.

chapters.title: Montgomery's Goodbye
chapters.description: As the losses mount in the final weeks, Colson Montgomery punctuates a forgettable season with his 20th home run, a rare reason to believe in what comes next.
